title: 'They shot to kill': Brother of Burk's Falls shooting victim expresses pain, anger
article: Sheena Jackson was in pain but she was starting to get back on her feet.
The 38-year-old mother who split her time between Oshawa and Burk's Falls had just suffered the loss of a child, for the second time.
"That's the second kid she's had to bury," her older brother Roger Jackson said of his niece, who died in June. "Her son died at six of brain cancer. She was going through a lot."
It is still unclear exactly what happened Aug. 5 when Almaguin OPP were called to Ye Olde Cutter Camp , a campground and trailer park where Sheena and her partner Devon Boston spent their summers.

SIU, now investigating the incident, say Sheena was wielding a knife when police encountered her at 8:19 p.m. A witness in the park who heard the next 11 minutes unfold said Sheena was shot by 8:30 p.m.
Multiple shots were fired from the guns of two officers, SIU confirmed.
The coroner told Sheena's mother Melanie she was shot twice in the heart, Roger said.
"They didn't have to do that," he said, questioning why a Taser wasn't used instead. "They shot to kill. They didn't shoot to disarm someone, they shot to kill."

Metroland spoke with members of Sheena's family who said Boston called police that night "like he has done before" because Sheena was in need of help. They said she had a "very small knife, one for peeling potatoes" that she was waving around because she did not want to go to the hospital.
"She's not a violent person," Roger said. "I don't want her painted like this bad person. She was amazing."

Living with the grief from the sudden death of her 20-year-old daughter Chloe, in June and the loss of her 6-year-old son Kurtis to brain cancer in 2010, had led to her having a nervous breakdown, he said.
Sheena was in Burk's Falls where she and Boston had a cabin at the park, after she had taken a week of leave from her job in Oshawa.
A week ago, at a family barbecue Roger said his sister was in good spirits, having just secured a new job following her daughter's funeral.

He understands that what happened in the moments before the shooting created a stressful situation for everyone present and that officers need to protect themselves but he said he has been told by people present that his sister was 15 to 25 feet away from the officers.
They are trained professionals, he said, and they did not handle the situation accordingly, in his opinion.
"I would like to know the whole story but we're not getting it," he said.
On Aug. 9 a protester sat outside the Almaguin OPP detachment in a lawn chair with two signs. One read, "Distress should (not equal) death" and the other, "Surely, there are options."
Matthew Orr, whose family owns the park, also said Boston was the one who called police. "The important thing that hasn't been conveyed is that it was a call regarding a mental health incident."
Roger, a father of three, put it plainly: "If you bury your daughter, you already bury your son, you wouldn't be in your right mind."
"She was murdered in my mind," he said. "We can't even trust the police anymore. They're supposed to protect, not kill."
